h6_rich_b1000.block:
[Interview, 2003-10-24, NEWS FROM CNN]
HOST: Thanks to both of you for joining us. Let's get right to Arnaud. You just got back from Pakistan. You were in the region for some time. What is the assessment out there about how the U.S. is doing in Iraq and Afghanistan?
GUEST: Well, I was having dinner the night before last with the chief minister of the northwest frontier province, who is an Islamist extremist...

HOST: In Pakistan.
GUEST: In Pakistan, head of the MMA (ph), which is his party, political religious coalition, and I quoted to him a story in the paper that morning and asked him, 'What do you think of this paper?" called "Nawa Eqat" (ph). And he said it's a very serious paper. And I said, 'Well, it's just reported that 4,000 Iraqi women were raped by Americans soldiers.' And he said, well, you guys have a way of suppressing that news.

HOST: And he actually believed it.
GUEST: He actually believed it.

HOST: And so, in other words, the image of the United States in Iraq in that part of the world, the Islamic world, is awful right now.
GUEST: Well, 80 percent of the people in Pakistan believe that Osama bin Laden is a freedom fighter and not a terrorist. And Osama...

HOST: Well, where do you get the number 80 percent? Are there any reliable polls there?
GUEST: Yes, they had a survey done in the northwest frontier province, for instance. And Osama's picture appears on page 3 every day in that same newspaper.

HOST: And, Larry, when you hear this kind of stuff, you know, I know that you've been critical of the administration for some time, but your blood must start boiling.

HOST: He's well known, Arnaud, as you well know, Donald Rumsfeld -- you and I have covered him for a long time -- as a taskmaster. He's very tough on the people who work for him.
GUEST: The root cause of all of the problems, as I think you would agree, is to listen to people like Ahmad Chalabi and the Iraqi National Congress who were telling their friends in the Pentagon, from Paul Wolfowitz on down, that this was going to be a very easy war, that millions of people were going to be waiting for us, they couldn't wait to be liberated, and that everything would go back...

HOST: So, you think Chalabi sold Rumsfeld a bill of goods.
GUEST: Oh, absolutely.

HOST: Do you agree, Larry?

HOST: We're talking about intelligence, the war in Iraq, the Rumsfeld memo. Chris from Florida, you're on the air. Go ahead with your question.

HOST: A fair point.

HOST: A fair...

HOST: All right, all right, we' got the point, Chris. Larry, that's a fair point. You have to admit, even though you're a tough critic of this administration, the world is better off with Saddam Hussein hiding out someplace rather than ruling Iraq.

HOST: Do you have doubts about that?

HOST: All right...

HOST: Midge, we have an e-mail. Milton in Florida writes this, see if you want to respond: "Bush, Powell and others by their lies or complete intelligence breakdown went to war in Iraq illegally. Neither the American people nor the rest of the world are able to trust the U.S. anymore." What do you say to Milton, Midge?

HOST: They still might...

HOST: All right.

HOST: Well, we know that the Rumsfeld memo was an authentic memo. He himself confirmed that that memo...

HOST: The one that was in "USA Today" this week. He admitted that...

HOST: That was written -- every word was written by him.

HOST: Elva in Canada has sent an e-mail. Let me let Arnaud handle this one. He knows the world about as well anyone. "Why is the U.S. and Spain asking other countries to cough up money for Iraq when it is the U.S. who caused the mess there in the first place? Why would countries who opposed the war donate billions of dollars to rebuild Iraq when the U.S. destroyed it?" Arnaud, this brings me to the Saudi Arabia subject you reported on this week. The Saudis can breathe a lot easier right now. Kuwait can breathe a lot easier right now. The oil-rich Arab states, the small ones, Bahrain, the UAE, Qatar, others there, they can all breathe a lot easier with Saddam Hussein gone. Why don't they cough up billions of dollars to help rebuild Iraq, thanks to the removal of Saddam Hussein?
GUEST: Well, I think what they see of the invasion of Iraq by the United States, as Larry pointed out, has caused hundreds of thousands of young Muslims to rally the cause against the Saudi regime, against the so-called Western puppets in that part of the world. And there is no reason that they should put up billions of dollars given the fact that they have now other problems to face, including what has just happened in the story I reported, which is the nuclear deal between Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, because they see across the Persian Gulf Iran. And they are convinced that Iran is not giving up its nuclear ambitions, has just temporarily postponed them.

HOST: We're going to speak to Khalid Al Maeena a reporter for the "Arab News". That's coming up in our next segment. But you're story, you're suggesting that there's a secret deal between Saudi Arabia and Pakistan involving nuclear weapons technology. Tell our viewers what you're reporting.
GUEST: I reported that as a result of Crown Prince Abdullah's visit to Islamabad last week, there was a deal with President Musharraf that in the future they didn't have to worry about being exposed in a nuclear sense because Pakistan would provide the nuclear umbrella one way or another. Now, of course it is denied.

HOST: Everybody is denying it.
GUEST: Of course. Well, look, President Zia, when he was the president of Pakistan, for 11 years lied to us about their own nuclear program. They said, No, we're not doing it.

HOST: Aslam? A-s-l-a-m?

HOST: OK and do you -- did they give another name -- Alsam?

HOST: Asthmatics and those with respiratory problems are at greater risk for health damage than the average New Yorker says Dr. Regina Santella.

HOST: Environmental watchdogs aren't so sure.

HOST: Kupferman filed a Freedom of Information Act request to get data about EPA's monitoring of pollutants. Data the EPA says Kupferman takes out of context.

HOST: But even experts admit there's no way to know for sure what the long-term effect of exposure to these pollutants will be. Brian Palmer, CNN, New York.

[Interview, 2002-05-13, AMERICAN MORNING WITH PAULA ZAHN]
HOST: We're going to talk more now about the search for Osama bin Laden and the relationship between the U.S. and Pakistan with a man who is just back from the region. Arnaud GUEST is an Editor-At-Large for both UPI and the "Washington Times." And we're delighted to see you in person for a change -- good morning.
GUEST: Thank you, Paula.

HOST: Do you see the U.S. acting unilaterally here at a time when unnamed U.S. sources are essentially saying they're not getting the cooperation for Pakistani they need right now to infiltrate that area and better understand what's going on in this population of 3.5 million people?
GUEST: I doubt it very much, because if we started acting unilaterally, it would be known to the Pakistan army. The Pakistani army would then leak it to some of their favorite newspapers in Pakistan, who -- the papers that are mostly anti-American, and the fat would be in the fire. You'd have riots all over Pakistan.

HOST: So tell us about the strategy that Barbara Starr just laid out prior to our interview. The idea of continuing to -- the British troops trying to flush the al Qaeda further south.
GUEST: I think the al Qaeda have great mobility. They move a lot at night. Not that we can't detect them, but they are in very small groups now. When Osama came across, apparently there were only 50 people with him, and they then got into smaller vehicles to drive into Peshawar. As for the next terrorist targets, nobody really knows. And I think a lot of this information has been put out by al Qaeda and its operatives to destabilize the United States, to demoralize the United States. My guess is that the next major terrorist movement will take place in the Persian Gulf, either in a Saudi oil terminal, a Saudi -- the nerve center of Saudi oil fields, which is called Abcaque (ph) -- or perhaps sinking a super tanker in the straights of Hormuz, which is very easily done at night from a rubber boat, sticking a bunch of limpid mines on the waterline of a super tanker. That's my guess, because Osama bin Laden understands that it's the economy, stupid, and anything tampering with oil in the Persian Gulf would discombobulate almost immediately oil markets and stock markets.

HOST: GUEST, thank you very much for dropping by in person. Appreciate your time.
GUEST: Thank you. TO ORDER A VIDEO OF THIS TRANSCRIPT, PLEASE CALL 800-CNN-NEWS OR USE OUR SECURE ONLINE ORDER FORM LOCATED AT www.fdch.com

[Interview, 2003-10-24, NEWS FROM CNN]
HOST: Today's "Hot Topics" panel discussion: The Senate panel, a scathing report about U.S. intelligence collected before the war in Iraq, the massive cost of post-war operations and the fruitless search, at least so far, for Osama bin Laden. Arnaud GUEST is the editor-at-large for "United Press International," one of the premiere international correspondents from around the world. He is joining us here in Washington, as is Laurence Korb. Lawrence Korb is now -- and correct if me if I'm wrong, Lawrence -- you're with the Center for American Progress, a former Pentagon official during the Reagan administration.

HOST: ... against a bunch of terrorists. How bad, in your assessment, was the intelligence, Arnaud, going into the war?
GUEST: I don't think it was that bad, frankly. I never heard tat we were going to find weapons of mass destruction. In fact, I heard just the opposite. And, as a matter of fact, the day the war started, I was in Amman seeing the former prime minister of Jordan. And I said, 'What if we don't find these weapons of mass destruction?' He said, well, you'd better invent them right way, because otherwise it's going to be disastrous.

HOST: All right, now, you're just back from Pakistan. You checked out the situation. Is al Qaeda and the Taliban, are they making a comeback in Afghanistan?

HOST: All right, I want to bring in another guest. Midge Decter is joining us now from New York. Midge Decter is the author of a new book, a biography of the secretary of defense, Donald Rumsfeld. The book is entitled, "Rumsfeld: a Personal Portrait." Midge, thanks very much for joining us. It looks like Donald Rumsfeld is getting a lot of bad publicity right now for that memo he wrote that was leaked to "USA Today" earlier this week, suggesting that the Defense Department, lo and behold, is not necessarily prepared for this war on terrorism.

HOST: All right, Arnaud...

HOST: Well, I think, in part, as you probably appreciate, Midge, it's because of the near daily casualties, the hundreds of American troops who have died since the start of the war, and the thousands of others who have either been seriously injured or maimed. And, as a result, the terrorism that continues to unfold there certainly gets the headlines. Let's get a caller, Midge and gentlemen guests.

HOST: Michael in New York has a question. Michael, go ahead.

HOST: All right, stand by, Arnaud, Larry, Midge. I'm going to take a quick break. We have a lot more to talk about, including more of your phone calls and your e-mail.

HOST: Arnaud...

HOST: Larry, what do you make of this story?

HOST: Progressive. Some would say liberal. Lawrence Korb, thanks very much for joining us. Arnaud, Midge, thank you very much. TO ORDER A VIDEO OF THIS TRANSCRIPT, PLEASE CALL 800-CNN-NEWS OR USE OUR SECURE ONLINE ORDER FORM LOCATED AT www.fdch.com.
